title: Errors Are Easy To Make
excerpt: Errors are easy to make when an interface leaves predictable mistakes accessible during normal operation. The failure is usually absent constraint, unclear guidance, or feedback that arrives too late to prevent the error.
metaDescription: A failure pattern where interfaces make predictable errors accessible during normal operation because constraints, guidance, or feedback are absent.
summary: This failure describes standard-use interface conditions that make predictable errors likely: missing pre-action validation, ambiguous feedback at decision points, and interface complexity that hides which element is operative.
definition: Errors are easy to make when the interface makes an incorrect action, selection, or input as accessible as the correct one during normal, intentional operation.

bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Errors are easy to make when an interface leaves the incorrect path too accessible relative to the correct one during normal, intentional operation. This failure occurs when the interface does not make valid and invalid actions legible before the user acts, does not constrain structurally invalid inputs, or does not provide feedback early enough for the user to detect a wrong step.

An interface that makes errors easy may still be technically complete. The system can perform all required functions correctly while providing inadequate scaffolding for users to navigate those functions without predictable mistakes. The failure is not that the software cannot execute the operation. The failure is that the interface does not communicate what the user should do clearly enough to prevent avoidable error.

The cost of this failure may appear as recurring support requests, high training effort, or an adoption ceiling for non-specialist users. The error itself may be only the visible symptom of a deeper design condition: the correct path has not been made substantially easier to identify and follow than the incorrect path.

## Errors-easy failures occur during standard operation, not only in rare scenarios

Errors-easy failures concern standard-use conditions that make predictable mistakes easy to commit. The user is on the designed path, has an intentional task, and is trying to operate the system correctly. The interface still permits or invites a wrong action because constraint, guidance, or feedback is insufficient.

This differs from rare-scenario interaction support. Rare-scenario failures concern what happens when the user is in a non-standard scenario or off the designed path. Errors-easy failures concern what happens when the user is on the designed path but the path is not designed to prevent predictable error.

Errors-easy failures also differ from unclear action scope. If the user has identified the right object and is looking at it, but a correct action reaches a different object, the relevant failure is that the interface does not make clear what an action will affect. Errors-easy failures cover the earlier discrimination problem: the user cannot reliably tell which of several similar elements is the right one to operate on.

## Absence of pre-action constraint and validation makes invalid actions available

The most preventable errors-easy condition is the absence of pre-action constraint and validation. The interface accepts an action or input that is structurally invalid for the current context, without communicating the invalidity before the user commits.

This condition appears when a user enters data in a format the operation cannot use, selects an element that is incompatible with the current operation, or begins a sequence that depends on a precondition that has not been met. The interface accepts the action, and the error occurs.

Pre-action constraint and validation are architecturally different from post-action error messages. A field that communicates accepted formats before entry, a column list that distinguishes operable from non-operable columns before selection, and a workflow that prevents progress until a necessary precondition is visible all change the structure of the decision. Each makes the correct action more accessible than the incorrect one before the user acts.

## Ambiguous feedback at decision points delays error detection

Errors become easier when the interface does not communicate clearly at the moment of action whether the action taken was the intended one. The user makes a selection, the interface updates, and the user cannot determine from the response whether the expected action occurred.

This condition is common where multiple actions are available and their differences are not visually or interactively clear. A user may not know whether they selected the right element, applied the right configuration, or completed a required step until a downstream consequence appears.

Late detection increases recovery cost because the origin of the error becomes harder to trace. The user may have to infer which earlier decision caused the current problem, rather than receiving clear feedback at the decision point itself.

## Interface complexity can hide which element is operative

An interface can make errors easy by hiding which visible element is currently relevant to the user’s intended action. The user knows what they want to do, but cannot reliably identify which element the action should be applied to.

This is a discrimination failure. Multiple elements appear similar, have similar visual weight, or depend on a system state that is not surfaced clearly. The user applies a correct intended action to the wrong element because the interface has not made the relevant element distinguishable.

This condition appears in data-heavy interfaces where visually similar columns serve different operational functions, where a column contains multiple types of content, or where the current operative element depends on an unsurfaced state. It also appears in information-dense content platforms where a user must distinguish the relevant regulatory item from many structurally similar items.

## Polymatica shows how missing operability guidance makes data-operation errors likely

Polymatica’s analytics platform required users to perform OLAP operations on imported datasets. Users had to identify the relevant column, apply the appropriate operation type, and obtain the intended analytical output.

Before the redesign, the interface did not distinguish which columns were operable for which operations and under what conditions. When users imported real datasets with mixed content, inconsistent formats, or values the system could not operate on for the intended purpose, the interface presented all columns without distinction.

The specific errors-easy condition was that users could not tell which column would support the intended operation, which column contained the issue preventing the operation, or what the issue was. Users attempted operations on columns that would not produce the intended result, received errors or unexpected outputs they could not interpret, and had no designed path to diagnosing or correcting the issue.

Creative Navy’s design response introduced a data preparation and preview step between data import and operations. Users could inspect their actual data before committing to operations, see a sample of column contents, rename columns to match their mental model, and identify structural inconsistencies before they produced downstream errors.

The available Polymatica evidence is calibrated. The messy-data failure mode, specifically the inability to identify which column to operate on, largely disappeared from support requests after the data preparation step was introduced. This was an observed operational change, not a measured error-rate reduction. The broader product analytics outcome, independent task completion moving from 2% to 40% and then 56%, includes but is not limited to the errors-easy improvement.

## Enhesa shows how dense content systems produce orientation and retrieval errors

Enhesa is a web-based legal compliance intelligence platform used by regulatory affairs managers, compliance officers, and legal teams. Users navigate baseline regulation pages that aggregate legislative text, implementation timelines, requirements, and changes for individual regulations across jurisdictions.

A systematic review of 95 session recordings produced a catalogue of 12 error types, each with a measured time-to-redress. Known error types included clicking into the wrong legislative text, creating the wrong filter, and missing a correct search result that was present in the system.

These were orientation and retrieval errors. Users were not necessarily misunderstanding their task. They were arriving at or acting on the wrong element because the interface did not make the relevant element sufficiently distinct from irrelevant elements at the moment of selection.

Creative Navy’s design response in the Enhesa engagement used three levels of intervention. Three error types were made structurally impossible by eliminating the interaction conditions that produced them. Five error types were made easier to recover from by providing clearer feedback and shorter correction paths. Six error types were expected to reduce in frequency because the correct path was made more visible and the incorrect path less accessible.

The Enhesa evidence is specific but bounded. The error types and workarounds were Creative Navy-recorded from session recording analysis during Sandbox Experiments. Of 31 documented workarounds, 80% were addressed in the redesign. The workaround density was concentrated in the primary content area, with 17 of 31 workarounds in Using legal texts. The post-redesign error outcomes were inferred from design decisions and were not independently measured after deployment.

## Creative Navy’s Critical Systems Design method identifies specific error points

Creative Navy’s Critical Systems Design method addresses errors-easy interfaces by identifying where and why errors occur, then changing the interface conditions so the correct path is substantially more accessible than the incorrect one.

Microtask analysis is the practice that makes error-point identification specific. A generic usability observation might say that users struggled with column selection. Microtask analysis turns that observation into a design requirement: users could not distinguish operable from non-operable columns because the interface presented all columns with equal visual treatment and provided no preview of what operations would produce with actual data.

In the Polymatica engagement, domain learning included Creative Navy performing operations on real data. That produced the messy-data column-identification problem as an experienced failure rather than only an inferred one. The resulting design requirement was that the interface must communicate column operability status before the user selects a column.

In the Enhesa engagement, Creative Navy used session recording analysis of 95 recorded usage sessions to document actual error patterns at scale. Time-to-redress added a cost dimension to each error type. The design requirement became specific: these 12 error types occur, each has a recovery cost, and each is produced by identifiable structural conditions.

## Raymarine illustrates the difference between selection error and transmitted error

Raymarine evidence concerns a measured discrimination error on a prototype bench fixture: selecting the wrong vessel from similar targets. The client is Raymarine, and its existing fixed-mount VHF line includes Ray53, Ray63 and Ray73. The new radio’s name is not used here.

Initial wrong target selections were four of eight under immediate calling and three of eight under confirmation. All three initial errors under the confirmation condition were detected and corrected at the confirmation screen before any request was sent. Wrong recipient submissions were two of eight under immediate calling and zero of eight under confirmation.

The Raymarine findings keep selection errors and transmitted errors separate. Confirmation did not prevent target selection mistakes. It made the recipient identity legible at a second decision point, giving operators the opportunity to detect and correct them before the request was submitted. The confirmation step removed a class of addressing error and cost 5.85 seconds and two and a half additional interactions.

Creative Navy designed the test protocols, moderated all twenty-four sessions and analysed the results. Raymarine supplied the physical bench mockup on which the sessions ran. Each comparison was paired and counterbalanced within participants, with task wording, target data and starting states held constant. The findings describe operator behaviour on a prototype against a fixed scenario fixture. They are not a measure of radio performance, real-world calling accuracy, or outcomes at sea.

## The handheld command-and-control engagement illustrates error invitations in touchscreen controls

The handheld command-and-control engagement was for a European manufacturer of uncrewed systems, including one-way effectors, and the tactical command-and-control software that operates them. Creative Navy designed the surface through which a human supervises the system; Creative Navy did not design the system.

The written failure-mode catalogue identified why a single touchscreen input is not an adequate commitment gate for an irreversible action. Touchscreens are vulnerable to accidental touches, rain and moisture, gloves, vibration and device movement, palm contact, selection of the wrong control under stress, and digitizer faults. The written case also records that an accidental strike command probably cannot be aborted inside the available window, particularly if the operator does not notice the error immediately.

Protection patterns such as slide-to-confirm, hold-to-commit at 300–600 ms, and select-then-arm were treated as substitute protection for size at T2 and below, never at T1, where size is the protection and is never substituted. The sizing specification measures itself against MIL-STD-1472 and states where it deliberately departs from it; it is not standards conformance.

The evidence is a written design argument, not a measured outcome. The co-authored case against the permanently visible control did not make the system safe and was not validated. The deliverable records that the hold duration and the physical-control design required human-factors and system-safety testing that was not performed. No accidental activation was counted before or after.

## visioncheckout shows observed checkout slips without redesign outcome claims

visioncheckout is a German vendor of computer-vision self-checkout systems for staff restaurants and catering. The relevant evidence consists of field observations of the current system being replaced, not counted events and not redesign results.

Observed slips included guests taking food away leaving the lid on and not knowing why recognition failed. An empty glass on the tray produced a charge alongside the drink it held; regular canteen users had learned to avoid this, while at the public venue staff intervened. An employee intending to pay by credit card forgot to present the employee card for the discount and paid more than they should.

These observations show how a routine interface can leave slips accessible when the required condition is not made visible or structurally protected at the moment of action. No percentage is attached to the observations, nothing about the redesigned product was tested, and no throughput, speed, error-rate, or accuracy outcome is claimed.

## Boundaries and limits of the errors-easy failure pattern

Errors-easy failures are not the same as recovery failures. An interface may still need strong recovery paths even after prevention has been improved. Prevention is the highest-value response where achievable, but easier recovery is appropriate where prevention would block legitimate use cases or impose unacceptable cost.

Errors-easy failures are also not evidence that users are careless. The pattern describes interface conditions that make predictable mistakes accessible. In the strongest cases, the user’s intended action is correct and the error arises because the interface has not made the valid object, valid input, or valid state legible enough before action.

The evidence across the examples has different strength. Polymatica includes product analytics for broader independent task completion, but the specific messy-data error improvement was observed through support-request change rather than measured as an error rate. Enhesa includes session recording analysis and documented time-to-redress, but post-redesign error outcomes were inferred from design decisions. Raymarine includes bench prototype counts, with stated limits. The handheld command-and-control material is a written design argument, not validation. visioncheckout observations are field observations of the system being replaced, not counted events or redesign outcomes.

## Related pages

This failure is closely related to errors that are hard to notice, errors that are hard to correct, weak recovery paths, and unclear action scope. It is also adjacent to rare-scenario interaction support, but the boundary is different: errors-easy failures concern predictable mistakes during normal operation, while rare-scenario failures concern non-standard scenarios.
